interest: For diplomatic and military historians, this file provides an extraordinarily rich, contemporaneous perspective from American diplomats on the ground in Tokyo during the pivotal year of 1938, as Japan shifted into total-war mobilization and openly repudiated the Open Door policy in favor of its 'New Order in East Asia.' The reports offer granular documentation of specific flashpoints—such as the presentation and payment of the $2.2 million USS Panay indemnity, the downing of a civilian CNAC airliner, the arrest of aviator Elwyn H. Gibbon, and the Changkufeng border battle with the USSR—illustrating the direct operational frictions threatening neutrality. Furthermore, the inclusion of internal Division of Far Eastern Affairs memoranda (such as Salisbury's analyses and the investigation into the reactionary Meinkokukai society) and exhaustive embassy transmission schedules offers valuable institutional insight into how the State Department processed, indexed, and evaluated intelligence on Japanese factional politics and economic controls.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.00, File 1169, Part 1 of 2) consists primarily of the comprehensive monthly political and economic reports (Reports Nos. 137 through 147) compiled and transmitted throughout 1938 by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew and the American Embassy in Tokyo to the Department of State, supplemented by internal Division of Far Eastern Affairs review memoranda and embassy communication logs. The documentation provides a systematic, month-by-month record of the intensifying Second Sino-Japanese War—including major military milestones such as the battle of Taierhchwang, the capture of Canton and Hankow, aerial bombings of commercial and mission properties, and the shooting down of a CNAC passenger airliner—alongside escalating diplomatic friction with the United States and Great Britain over Yangtze River navigation, treaty rights, assaults on foreign nationals, and the resolution of the USS Panay indemnity claim. Concurrently, the file chronicles Japan's internal transformation under Prime Minister Fumimaro Konoe, detailing the passage and enforcement of the National General Mobilization Law, Cabinet reshuffles and resignations (notably Foreign Minister Kazushige Ugaki), crackdowns on domestic liberalism, deadlocked Soviet-Japanese fisheries talks and the Changkufeng border clash, and Japan's formal challenge to the Open Door doctrine through its proclamation of a 'New Order in East Asia.'
